chunks: And the one who narrated it: Muhammad ibn Yahya from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn from Muhammad ibn Abdillah ibn Hilal from Uqbah ibn Khalid, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who performed Tamattu' and did not have what to buy a sacrifice with. When he fasted three days during Hajj and then became financially able, should he buy a sacrifice and slaughter it, or leave that and fast seven days when he returns to his family? He said: 'He buys a sacrifice and slaughters it, and the fasting he already performed becomes voluntary (nafl) for him.'

This report is understood as indicating recommendation (istihbab) and preference (nadab), because whoever finds the price of the sacrifice after having fasted some days has the choice: if he wishes, he fasts the remainder of what is upon him, and if he wishes, he slaughters the sacrifice. And whoever cannot find the sacrifice, it is obligatory upon him to fast ten days: three during Hajj and seven when he returns to his family.
Allah, the Exalted, said: 'So whoever cannot find [a sacrifice] - then a fast of three days during Hajj and seven when you have returned. Those are ten complete [days].'

key_terms.تَمَتَّعَ: Performed Tamattu' Hajj (combining Umrah and Hajj)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling for a pilgrim who cannot afford the Hajj sacrifice after fasting some days?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi contextualizes this narration by interpreting the Prophet’s response as indicating that the initial three days of fasting are merely recommended (mustahabb) rather than obligatory, allowing the pilgrim to substitute them with the sacrifice upon gaining means. This ruling highlights the Shia jurisprudential principle of flexibility in expiation (kaffarah), distinguishing between the mandatory ten-day fast and the optional nature of the preliminary fasting period. The text explicitly links this legal mechanism to the Quranic verse, reinforcing the conditionality of the sacrifice based on financial capacity.
